claims.text: Thermal exposure of the metastable Mg-containing lightweight HEA activates atomic diffusion.
Thermally activated diffusion causes breakdown of local supersaturation in the metastable solid solution.
Microstructural evolution is governed by diffusion-driven precipitation of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
The precipitated Mg-rich intermetallic compounds may include Laves or B2 phases.
The intermetallic compounds nucleate and grow both at grain boundaries and within grains.
Thermal exposure increases the volume fraction of intermetallic compounds relative to the initial metastable state.
Intermetallic particles disrupt the continuity of the protective solid-solution matrix.
Intermetallic precipitation locally depletes corrosion- and oxidation-resistant elements from the matrix.
Matrix disruption, galvanic coupling, and depletion of protective elements reduce corrosion resistance.
Matrix disruption and depletion of protective elements reduce high-temperature oxidation resistance.
After thermal exposure, corrosion current density will be higher than in the initial metastable state.
After thermal exposure, oxidation mass gain will be higher than in the initial metastable state.
The initial homogeneous distribution of protective elements gives the metastable solid-solution state higher corrosion and oxidation resistance.
The proposed pathway applies during exposure at approximately 400–700°C for durations ranging from hours to weeks.
The pathway does not apply below the threshold for significant diffusion or to alloys stabilized against intermetallic formation.
